newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-RYDER CAPTAIN KITE CONFOUNDED BY OPTIONS FOR U.S. UNDERDOGS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-RYDER CAPTAIN KITE CONFOUNDED BY OPTIONS FOR U.S. UNDERDOGS.

text.p: Captain Tom Kite is confounded by Ryder Cup options with six weeks to go before making a pair of picks to complete a U.S. team he says will be underdogs against Europe.
"I would love to have one or two guys step forward and make it real easy for me. To be honest, I don't know where I'm going to go," Kite told reporters this week.
"The decision is going to be incredibly difficult."
Kite will announce his captain's choices for the September 26-28 matches at Valderrama in Sotogrande, Spain, following the PGA Championship next month at Winged Foot.

Since the top 10 points earners in Ryder Cup standings gain automatic berths on the squad, Kite will be rounding out a team sure to be shy of Ryder Cup experience. The top 15 on the current list have played in a total of nine Ryder Cups.
Names such as Tommy Tolles, Jim Furyk and Scott Hoch -- all would-be Ryder rookies -- dot the top 10 list.

By contrast, Nick Faldo, a likely pick by European captain Seve Ballesteros, has played in 10 Cups himself, while Bernhard Langer and Ian Woosnam, both in solid position in Europe's standings, have played in 15 Cups between them.
"We have to be considered the underdogs," said Kite, who added that nothing can prepare a player for the level of pressure felt in the heat of Ryder Cup competition.

Kite, of course, will not be travelling to Spain unarmed as he has a number of formidable players lining up to take part including British Open champion Tom Lehman, Masters winner Tiger Woods and Mark O'Meara, with Phil Mickelson and Davis Love positioned to snag berths with some good finishes.
But Kite said the Valderrama layout, designed by Ballesteros, will also work to the Americans' disadvantage.

"We will have basically three days to learn everything there is to know about a golf course that they know like the back of their hand," said Kite, trying to wrest away the Cup that Europe won with a rousing Sunday singles comeback on enemy soil two years ago at Oak Hill.
"This golf course requires as much local knowledge as any golf course I've ever seen, including Augusta," commented the compact Texan.

"The dominant feature on this course is trees, oak trees. They are kind of like Texas live oaks. They don't have huge height, but they are twisted and gnarled and have these branches that hang out," said Kite, pointing out that European number one Colin Montgomerie has said it took him six years to figure out how best to play the course.

"There will be numerous times in this tournament where a player will be in the fairway and not have a clear shot to the green or to the pin. They will have to work it around the trees -- up or down, left or right to get around the trees."

Kite said prospective players including Woods, Lehman, Tolles, Steve Jones, John Cook and Payne Stewart were going to play Valderrama Sunday following next week's Loch Lomond event. O'Meara, Love and David Duvall planned to head to Valderrama that same weekend after a fishing trip together in Ireland.
The U.S. captain said an advance look would make for more productive practice once the team arrives for the match play event.

Kite said his team is shaping up similarly to the squad that qualified last time under U.S. captain Lanny Wadkins, who was criticised for naming old friend Curtis Strange to add some veteran seasoning for the 1995 matches.
Strange had won the 1989 U.S. Open at Oak Hill, but had fallen off form and was a controversial choice. Strange lost all three of his matches as Europe prevailed 14 1/2 to 13 1/2.

"It's not a whole lot unlike what Lanny was facing," Kite said about the experience factor on this team. But he added that unlike Wadkins, he seems sure to have a number of players he is close to and can bounce ideas off, including Lehman, Love and O'Meara.
Still, Kite would love to see a veteran step up, such as Corey Pavin, the toughest U.S. competitor on recent Ryder Cup teams, who is languishing in 36th place on the list.
The perplexed Kite, however, seems clear on one thing -- he's not apt to play his own way onto the U.S. team despite its lack of experience.
"The last couple of weeks, I find myself getting on the golf course and I'm no more thinking about playing golf than I am flying over the moon," said Kite, 28th on the list.
"My concentration wavers. I'm thinking about this. For the next couple of months I've got to put my own game on the back burner."
Kite, a veteran of seven Ryder Cups with an enviable record of 15-9-4, has said he would have to be playing great golf to consider making himself a playing captain.
"I think it would be a pretty gutsy play to pick myself. That would be like hitting a 2-iron from a downhill lie out of a divot to an elevated green with a tucked flagstick over a water hazard."
